title: Bernard and the Cistercians
hookLine: plain white habits, plain churches, farming and prayer

cards: How does a hard way of life survive when almost nobody wants to join it? A new monastery in a remote place called Cîteaux, in Burgundy, is struggling.
Its monks want to keep the Rule of Saint Benedict to the letter: their own manual work, plain food, plain clothes, long prayer. The early account says few came to join them.
Then a young nobleman knocks at the gate, and he hasn't come alone. He's brought brothers, relatives and friends, a whole company, all asking to become monks. His name is Bernard.
Before long he's sent out to found a new house in a valley called Clairvaux.

teach.h: THE WHITE MONKS STRIP THINGS BACK.
teach.b: The Cistercians, named for Cîteaux, wanted to strip things back. Their habits were plain undyed wool, pale enough that people called them the white monks. Their churches kept to bare walls and plain glass.
They farmed their own land, often in out-of-the-way valleys, and prayed the hours between the work. Bernard put the reason into sharp words.

In an essay to a friend, known as his Apology, he looked at the grand churches of other monasteries, with soaring heights, costly decoration and carved monsters on the cloister columns, and asked what it was all for.

teach.h: WALLS SHINE, AND THE POOR GO WITHOUT.
teach.b: In paraphrase: the church's walls shine, and its poor go without. It dresses its stones in gold and leaves its children naked. He wasn't against beauty.
He wrote tender sermons on the Song of Songs, full of longing for God. He was against distraction, and against spending on stone what the hungry needed.
Plainness, for the Cistercians, was its own kind of beauty: light through plain glass, stone and proportion with nothing to hide behind. Some readers hear an echo of a Gospel picture.
Jesus, in the King James words: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin." Nothing added, nothing missing. And, as yesterday, honesty.

teach.h: A SAINT WHO PREACHED A CRUSADE.
teach.b: Bernard also preached a crusade. He also wrote that the Jews must not be attacked, and he stood against a monk who was stirring up violence against them. Catholics honor him as a saint.

how: Cistercian monks and nuns, including the stricter Trappists, still keep the Rule of Saint Benedict in plain churches, supporting themselves by work such as farming, baking and brewing between the hours of prayer.

games.q: you're Bernard, writing to a friend about grand monastery churches full of gold and carved monsters. what do you say?
o: the grander the church, the greater the praise.
the walls shine, while the poor go without.
games.why: in his Apology, Bernard says the church dresses its stones in gold and leaves its children naked. plainness, for him, made room for God and for the poor.

practice: Choose one small space near you, a desk, a shelf, the screen in your hand, and look at it the way a Cistercian might look at a church: what here is helping, and what's only shouting for attention?
Gently take one or two things away, then sit with the plainer space a while and notice what's easier to see. If you pray, let the cleared space become a place for prayer.

wordCard.voice: Cistercians. The white monks of Cîteaux and Clairvaux, led by the abbot Bernard, who argued that plainness leaves room for God, and bread for the poor.

carryVoice: Your line: plainness is beautiful. Light through plain glass is still light. Day eight hundred eleven.
